tier_reason: These are first-party numbers, with no paper or independent suite, so tier B does not apply. The repo has runnable benchmark code (benchmark/benchmark.cpp) that calls std::sort, std::stable_sort and their std::execution::par versions, and benchmark_output.txt gives the hardware (i9-9900K 4.7GHz, DDR4-3000) and compiler ('Microsoft Visual C++ 2022, release mode'). No compiler flags or project file are given, so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README, 1 billion int32: radix_sort 6402ms vs std::sort 91407ms (README says '14.28x faster than std::sort') and vs std::stable_sort 82896ms (~12.9x). The README sets the parallel figure (radix_sort(par) 2603ms) only against single-threaded std::sort. benchmark/benchmark_output.txt shows std::sort(par) at 12537ms, so parallel against parallel is ~4.8x. The gain is smaller for wider keys. At 1e9 elements single-threaded it is ~5.2x for uint64 (17831ms vs 91867ms) and ~2.9x for pair<uint64,uint64> (33830ms vs 96751ms). In parallel on pair<uint64,uint64>, radix_sort(par) is slightly slower than std::sort(par) (24608ms vs 23532ms). The README headline range is '2.5-14.3x faster than std::sort'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Microsoft Visual C++ 2022, release mode (per benchmark/benchmark_output.txt); exact compiler flags not stated and no project file in repo
corrections.workload: benchmark/benchmark.cpp: 1e6, 1e7, 1e8 and 1e9 uniformly random int, uint64, pair<int,uint32> and pair<uint64,uint64> (first-key) elements, 5 rounds averaged. Covers std::sort, std::stable_sort and radix_sort, both sequential and with std::execution::par. The README headline uses 1e9 int32.
corrections.caveats: Single-author project, unmaintained since Jan 2022. Only MSVC STL was tested (no libstdc++/libc++), and exact MSVC flags are not stated. The README's parallel figure sets parallel radix_sort against sequential std::sort; against std::sort(par) the win is ~4.8x for int32. The speedup falls for 64-bit and pair keys, and parallel radix_sort is slightly slower than std::sort(par) on pair<uint64,uint64>.

notes: The headline numbers on the README match exactly. Tier goes from B to C because this is a first-party benchmark with no stated flags. The '~35.1x parallel' claim was an unfair comparison (parallel vs sequential) and has been corrected with the std::sort(par) data from the repo's benchmark_output.txt. License (GPL-3.0), 33 stars, last commit 2022-01-31 and 'abandoned' status are all confirmed.

tier_reason: The author's own benchmark code (src/bench.c, from the wolfsort suite) calls std::stable_sort directly, and the compiler and flags are stated (g++ 7.5.0 -O3 -w -fpermissive). The CPU is never stated, so it cannot be A. There is no paper or independent suite (for example, the cpp-sort benchmarks do not include quadsort), so B does not apply.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ~2.4x faster than std::stable_sort (g++ 7.5 libstdc++) on random arrays of 513-1024 32-bit ints: best 0.005664s vs 0.013871s (weighted benchmark, 50 samples). Across random arrays of 1-4096 items the gain is ~2.0-4.9x. The README's 100,000-element per-distribution data table labels its rows 'fluxsort', not quadsort, although the bar graph says quadsort. That table shows ~4.1x for ascending saw and ~5.5x for pipe organ, and ~15-16x only for fully ascending or descending input. It is slower than std::stable_sort on bit reversal, which the graph also shows for quadsort. The earlier '~16x ascending-saw / ~10x pipe-organ' figures are not supported.
corrections.workload: From the wolfsort bench.c: std::stable_sort vs quadsort vs timsort on 100,000 elements (32/64/128-bit) across 11 distributions (random, random%100, ascending, ascending saw, pipe organ, descending, descending saw, random tail, random half, ascending tiles, bit reversal), 100 samples with best and average reported. A second run covers random arrays of 1-4096 32-bit items (weighted repetitions, 50 samples).
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (the author's wolfsort suite, src/bench.c), not independently replicated. The CPU/hardware is never stated, only WSL2/Ubuntu 18.04 with GCC 7.5.0 (dated). The README's 100,000-element data table is mislabeled 'fluxsort' while its graph says quadsort, so per-distribution numbers for quadsort itself are unreliable. Quadsort is slower than std::stable_sort on bit-reversal input. It is C code, usable from C++ via its header.

notes: The 1024-item 2.4x figure is verified. The partially-ordered claims (16x/10x) were wrong and came from a table the README labels 'fluxsort'. Tier goes from B to C (first-party, no hardware stated). Metadata is confirmed: Unlicense, 2204 stars, last commit 2024-07-27, 'stale'.

tier_reason: The README numbers (hardware: Ryzen 3950X) come from the June 2020 benchmark bench/BM_fullsort.int64_t.cpp at commit ec12899. That code compares against gcsort::introsort_orig, a scalar port of the .NET CoreCLR GC introsort, not std::sort. The compiler and version are not stated, and that benchmark and baseline are no longer in master. Numbers without a reproducible run against the named baseline put this at C.

corrections.baseline: scalar introsort ported from the .NET CoreCLR GC (gcsort::introsort_orig), not std::sort
corrections.claimed_speedup: The README compares against 'Introspective Sort (Scalar Baseline)', which is a port of the .NET CoreCLR GC introsort sorting 64-bit pointers, not std::sort. It reports roughly 4.8x at 1M int64 with 8x unroll (55ns -> 11.5ns per element; the table gives 53.08ns vs 11.54ns, ~4.6x) and ~4.5x at 128K int64 (45ns -> 10.5ns). No std::sort numbers are published, and the int32 results have no baseline numbers.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler/version not stated (README recommends clang). CMakeLists defaults to a Release build. At the June 2020 commit behind the published results, Release flags for GCC/Clang were '-Ofast -DNDEBUG'; current master uses '-O2 -fomit-frame-pointer -DNDEBUG'.
corrections.workload: Single-core sorting of 4,096 to 1,048,576 elements. For int64, vxsort (AVX2, unroll 1/4/8/12) is compared against a scalar introsort on 64-bit pointer arrays. The int32 tables cover vxsort only (unroll 1/4/8), with no baseline.
corrections.caveats: The published baseline is not std::sort. It is gcsort::introsort_orig, a scalar port of the .NET CoreCLR GC introsort, from the 2020 code (bench/BM_fullsort.int64_t.cpp at ec12899). Current master has bench/fullsort/BM_fullsort.stdsort.cpp, which calls std::sort, but no std::sort results are published. The README results date from 2020 and no longer match the current benchmark code. The compiler version is not stated. The Ryzen 3950X (Zen 2) has no AVX-512, so the published numbers are AVX2 only. The default branch was last committed on 2023-05-10. Recent activity (2026-06-12) is on an unrelated-history 'nextgen' branch.
